subject: how to fit time series with both hour-by-hour and week-by-week variation

messages.author: 4cef6eb14d12f9f6
messages.subject: how to fit time series with both hour-by-hour and week-by-week variation
parts:
This isn't a Stan question per se, it's really a question about the best way to set up a specific type of model. I certainly won't resent it if you declare this to be outside the scope of this group.  At the same time, I would really appreciate some help, even (or perhaps especially) if you can just point me to an example model that does what I need.. 

I've made a toy problem. R code to simulate some data, and Stan code to fit a model, are below. The Stan model only does half of what I want, as I now describe.

I have a time series with a pattern that recurs weekly...except it doesn't quite recur weekly, each week is slightly different from the week before. There's also some stochastic variability. 

I would like to make use of the fact that I know that the underlying value varies smoothy from one hour to the next, and ALSO the fact that it varies smoothly from one week to the next (that is, if I look exactly one week earlier or later, the value won't be very different from what it is now). 

Here's what happens in the toy problem:
1. In R, I create a variable beta[week,hour] that varies smoothly in each direction. There's nothing special about the function I used, it could be anything really.
2. Using that matrix of betas, I create a time series, yy, that has the patterns in it.
3. I add noise to create yy_meas

The model below exploits the smoothness in one "dimension" (from one time to the next within a week) but not the other (the same time of the week, from one week to the next), as you can see in the "transformed parameters" section.

I can think of a few ways to impose or exploit the smoothness in both directions, but neither does what I really want, which is to say that I think the magnitude change from one time to the next within a week should be, say, student_t(4,0,sigma_1), and from one week to the next at the same time should be student_t(4,0,sigma_2). 

If there's a standard way to handle this --- or even a non-standard one --- I'd love to learn it. 

--Phil  



### Make fake data
Weeks = 8
Times_Per_Week = 5*24
NN = Weeks * Times_Per_Week
week = rep(1:Weeks,each=Times_Per_Week)
time_of_week = rep(1:Times_Per_Week,Weeks)

T_midweek = Times_Per_Week/2
beta_true = matrix(NA,nrow=Weeks,ncol=Times_Per_Week)
for (i_week in 1:Weeks) {
  for (i_time_of_week in 1:Times_Per_Week) {
    beta_true[i_week,i_time_of_week] = 
      150*dnorm(i_time_of_week,mean=T_midweek,sd=Times_Per_Week/(2+i_week/2))/(2+i_week/2)
  } 
}

yy = rep(NA,NN)
for (ii in 1:NN) {
  yy[ii] = beta_true[week[ii],time_of_week[ii]]
}  

plot(yy)

plot(time_of_week,yy,type="l",col=week)


### yy_meas is the "measured" data; we want to extract the underlying
###  yy as well as we can
yy_meas = yy + rnorm(n=NN,mean=0,sd=0.08)

par(mfrow=c(3,1))

plot(yy)
plot(yy_meas)
plot(time_of_week,yy,type="l",col=week)



####

#### Model:
ts_test_code <- '
data{
int N; // number of data points
int Weeks; // number of weeks
int Times_Per_Week; 
int week[N]; // week number for each data point
int time_of_week[N]; // day number for each data point
vector [N] y; //  data
}
parameters {
  vector [Times_Per_Week] gamma[Weeks]; //     
}

transformed parameters {
  vector [Times_Per_Week] beta_est[Weeks];
  vector [N] ypred;
  for (iw in 1:Weeks) {
    beta_est[iw,1] <- 0;
    for (jt in 2:Times_Per_Week) {
       beta_est[iw,jt] <- beta_est[iw,jt-1] + gamma[iw,jt];
    }
  }
  for (i in 1:N) {
    ypred[i] <- beta_est[week[i],time_of_week[i]];
  }     
}

model {
 for (iw in 1:Weeks) {
   gamma[iw] ~ student_t(8,0,0.08);
 }  
 y ~ normal(ypred,0.08);
}
'

stan_test_dat <- list(N=NN, y=yy_meas, Weeks=Weeks, Times_Per_Week=Times_Per_Week,
  week=week, time_of_week=time_of_week)

fit_test <- stan(model_code = ts_test_code, data=stan_test_dat,
iter=1000,warmup=800,chains=3,verbose=TRUE)

test_extract = extract(fit_test,permuted=F)
test_summary = summary(fit_test)

#### Plot a few things

plot(test_extract[,1,"lp__"],type="l",ylim=range(pretty(test_extract[,,"lp__"])))
lines(test_extract[,2,"lp__"],col="red")
lines(test_extract[,3,"lp__"],col="green")


plot(yy_meas)
lines(yy,col="blue")
iwhich = grep("ypred",rownames(test_summary$summary))
lines(test_summary$summary[iwhich,"50%"],col="orange")

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: how to fit time series with both hour-by-hour and week-by-week variation

On Sunday, February 17, 2013 4:29:25 PM UTC-5, Phil Price wrote:
This isn't a Stan question per se, it's really a question about the best way to set up a specific type of model. I certainly won't resent it if you declare this to be outside the scope of this group.  At the same time, I would really appreciate some help, even (or perhaps especially) if you can just point me to an example model that does what I need.

If the problem requires smoothness at midnight --- i.e. 11PM is smoothly related to 12AM the next day --- that is often modeled with circular statistics; see

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directional_statistics

Unfortunately, Stan doesn't have any circular densities implemented in C++ yet. Someone was working on a branch to implement them a while ago but I haven't seen or heard anything about its progress recently. In principle, any density can be represented in Stan code by manipulating the lp__ symbol directly, but the normalizing terms of circular densities often involve Bessel functions and things like that which may not be implemented in Stan yet either.

If Stan had more support for circular statistics, then I think the problem you outline could be handled by specifying some circular stuff for the hours. You could do the same for the days of the week, but that depends on how smoothly you think the Friday to Monday transition is. Alternatively, you might be able to just estimate an unstructured mean vector for each day of the week with hourly deviations from that mean that are smooth.

Ben

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] how to fit time series with both hour-by-hour and week-by-week variation
parts:
Phil:

What Ben said.  It would be no problem to "manually" put in dependence to impose smoothness however we'd like, but once we go beyond sequential or nested models (i.e., models than be factored, as with autoregressions), we also need to compute the normalizing factor as a function of the hyperparameters.

But . . . if your prior distribution (that is, your model on theta_1,…,theta_T) is Gaussian, then it's just a Gaussian process, which means that (a) the normalizing factor is based on the determinant of the covaraince matrix (thus, no bessel functions) and (b) it can be implemented using the Gaussian process in Stan.

Also, anything that's a straight time series can be trivially modeled using a random walk or AR model, in which case it just goes directly into the model, e.g., theta[t] ~ normal (mu + rho*(theta[t-1]-mu), sigma).

In your case, maybe it would be possible to decompose beta into different pieces corresponding to date, day-of-week, and hour-of-day.  The latter have just 7 and 24 dimensions so it's no big deal to put in Gaussian process.

A

parts: But . . . if your prior distribution (that is, your model on theta_1,…,theta_T) is Gaussian, then it's just a Gaussian process, which means that (a) the normalizing factor is based on the determinant of the covaraince matrix (thus, no bessel functions) and (b) it can be implemented using the Gaussian process in Stan.
Alas, my real problem is non-Gaussian: the change from one week to the next is almost always small, but on rare occasion it's very big. I really need to use a long-tailed distribution.

Also, anything that's a straight time series can be trivially modeled using a random walk or AR model, in which case it just goes directly into the model, e.g., theta[t] ~ normal (mu + rho*(theta[t-1]-mu), sigma).
I think this is equivalent to the way I modeled it in my toy problem, no? Except the way you have it here is slower (computationally)?

In your case, maybe it would be possible to decompose beta into different pieces corresponding to date, day-of-week, and hour-of-day.  The latter have just 7 and 24 dimensions so it's no big deal to put in Gaussian process.

Yeah, except the time-of-day effect needs to vary from one week to the next, which is where this whole thing comes from.

For now I am modeling the usually-small change from one week to the next, but not the change from one time of day to the next (the opposite of the toy problem). I'd like to do both at once. 

The following does not work, but why not? (Skipping the loops and declarations etc.; beta[a,b] are my parameters, deltas are transformed parameters):

delta_timeToTime[week,time_of_week] <- beta[week,time_of_week] - beta[week,time_of_week-1]
delta_weekToWeek[week,time_of_week] <- beta[week,time_of_week]-beta[week-1,time_of_week]

delta_timeToTime[week,time_of_week] ~ student_t(4,0,sigma1)
delta_weekToWeek[week,time_of_week] ~ student_t(4,0,sigma2)

Such a model compiles and runs but (in the cases I've tried) it won't take a step, the betas are frozen in place. Is this just a computational issue, it just can't find a good step, or am I conceptualizing this wrong?

Phil

Interesting.

I'm not too worried about smoothness at midnight, or across the boundary from one week to the next. I feel like my problem has a spatial-statistics character to it: if you just plot the surface of beta[week,time-of-week] then I think it should be smooth-ish in both dimensions (although not equally smooth in both). 

 I'll poke around in the "circular statistics" literature, thanks.

parts: You'll need to provide more context.

On 2/18/13 2:08 PM, Phil Price wrote:
>
> For now I am modeling the usually-small change from one week to the next, but not the change from one time of day to the
> next (the opposite of the toy problem). I'd like to do both at once.
>
> The following does not work, but why not? (Skipping the loops and declarations etc.; beta[a,b] are my parameters, deltas
> are transformed parameters):
>
> delta_timeToTime[week,time_of_week] <- beta[week,time_of_week] - beta[week,time_of_week-1]
> delta_weekToWeek[week,time_of_week] <- beta[week,time_of_week]-beta[week-1,time_of_week]
>
> delta_timeToTime[week,time_of_week] ~ student_t(4,0,sigma1)
> delta_weekToWeek[week,time_of_week] ~ student_t(4,0,sigma2)
>
> Such a model compiles and runs but (in the cases I've tried) it won't take a step, the betas are frozen in place. Is
> this just a computational issue, it just can't find a good step, or am I conceptualizing this wrong?

Excerpting the key idea helps, but we always need to see the
full models. What's the distribution on beta or on sigma?
Are the sigma1 and sigma2 constrained to be positive?

What you need to do is make sure the total log probability
over the parameters is defined properly.

a ~ foo(theta);

is translated in Stan the same way as:

lp__ <- lp__ + foo_log(a,theta);

This lets you calculate the total log probability.

This approach is OK conceptually as far as Stan's concerned, but
you need to account for the log absolute Jacobian determinant of
the transform from beta to (detal_timeToTime, delta_weekToWeek) to
make sure you get the right distribution on the beta. I'm still
not that good at this, or I'd work it out here in the e-mail.

Also, there must be some boundary conditions somewhere so that
time_of_week-1 and week-1 don't go below 1.

- Bob

Perhaps could be Gaussian with non-Gaussian additive errors?  Or a non-Gaussian random walk model?  Any model that is random walk or autoregressive can be expressed sequentially, hence no worry about the normalizing function.  The only part of the model that really seems difficult are the circular parts, so if _they_ could be Gaussian, you could go to town on the other parts.
A
